claim: TIR-1 is the C. elegans homolog of SARM1/dSarm.
source: Here we show that TIR-1/dSarm/SARM1, a key regulator of axon degeneration, also inhibits regeneration of injured motor axons.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states TIR-1 is related to dSarm and SARM1 in the abstract and introduction, and Figure 1A shows structural conservation.

claim: TIR-1 inhibits axon regeneration of injured motor axons.
source: Here we show that TIR-1/dSarm/SARM1, a key regulator of axon degeneration, also inhibits regeneration of injured motor axons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased regeneration in tir-1 mutants (Figure 1D).

claim: The increased regeneration in tir-1 mutants is not a secondary consequence of its effects on degeneration.
source: The increased regeneration in tir-1 mutants is not a secondary consequence of its effects on degeneration, nor is it determined by the NADase activity of TIR-1.
evidence: Supported by data showing tir-1 mutants regenerate more after single injury where degeneration does not occur.

claim: The increased regeneration in tir-1 mutants is not determined by the NADase activity of TIR-1.
source: The increased regeneration in tir-1 mutants is not a secondary consequence of its effects on degeneration, nor is it determined by the NADase activity of TIR-1.
evidence: Supported by data showing E788A and D773A mutations do not affect regeneration (Figure 5A).

claim: TIR-1 functions cell-autonomously to regulate axon regeneration and degeneration.
source: Rather, we found that TIR-1 functions cell-autonomously to regulate each of the seemingly opposite processes through distinct interactions with two MAP kinase pathways.
evidence: Supported by GABA-specific rescue experiments (Figure 2E, 3H).

claim: TIR-1 inhibits axon regeneration by activating the NSY-1/ASK1 MAPK signaling cascade.
source: On one side of the injury, TIR-1 inhibits axon regeneration by activating the NSY-1/ASK1 MAPK signaling cascade, while on the other side of the injury, TIR-1 simultaneously promotes axon degeneration by interacting with the DLK-1 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling cascade.
evidence: Supported by genetic epistasis data showing nsy-1 and pmk-1 mutants phenocopy tir-1 regeneration phenotype (Figure 5C).

claim: TIR-1 promotes axon degeneration by interacting with the DLK-1 MAPK signaling cascade.
source: On one side of the injury, TIR-1 inhibits axon regeneration by activating the NSY-1/ASK1 MAPK signaling cascade, while on the other side of the injury, TIR-1 simultaneously promotes axon degeneration by interacting with the DLK-1 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling cascade.
evidence: Supported by genetic data showing dlk-1 and pmk-3 suppress tir-1 degeneration phenotype (Figure 7B).

claim: The ability to cell-intrinsically inhibit axon regeneration is conserved in human SARM1.
source: In parallel, we found that the ability to cell-intrinsically inhibit axon regeneration is conserved in human SARM1.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with human SARM1 SAM-TIR domain (Figure 2F).

claim: In the central nervous system and in aged animals, regeneration of the proximal axon fragment is inhibited, resulting in a permanent loss of neuronal function.
source: However, in the central nervous system and in aged animals, regeneration of the proximal axon fragment is inhibited, resulting in a permanent loss of neuronal function (Cai et al., 2001; David and Aguayo, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SARM1/dSarm is essential for injury-induced axon degeneration of mouse and fly axons.
source: On the distal side of the injury, the most notable endogenous regulator of axon degeneration is Sterile Alpha and toll/interleukin-1 resistance (TIR) motif containing 1 (SARM1/dSarm), which is essential for injury-induced axon degeneration of mouse and fly axons (Gerdts et al., 2013; Osterloh et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SARM1/dSarm promotes axon degeneration cell-autonomously by depleting NAD+.
source: SARM1/dSarm promotes axon degeneration cell-autonomously by depleting NAD+, interacting with the BTB/BACK domain protein Axundead, and interacting with mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling cascades, which in turn regulate calpain activation, SCG10/Stathmin-2 proteolysis, mitochondrial dysfunction, cytoskeletal disruption, and axon fragmentation (Coleman and Höke, 2020; Essuman et al., 2017; Gerdts et al., 2015; Gerdts et al., 2016; Neukomm et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2012; Summers et al., 2020; Walker et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TIR-1 was first characterized as a determinant of neuronal asymmetry and the innate immune response.
source: The Caenorhabditis elegans SARM1/dSarm homolog, TIR-1, was first characterized as a determinant of neuronal asymmetry and the innate immune response, which it regulates in coordination with the NSY-1/ASK1 MAPK signaling pathway (Chuang and Bargmann, 2005; Couillault et al., 2004; Liberati et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TIR-1 regulates neurodegeneration in response to disease and age, upon multimerization, and in the absence of mitochondria.
source: In the absence of injury, TIR-1 has been found to regulate neurodegeneration in response to disease and age, upon multimerization, and in the absence of mitochondria (Ding et al., 2022; Lezi et al., 2018; Loring et al., 2021; Vérièpe et al., 2015); however, whether TIR-1 regulates injury-induced axon degeneration is not known.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: More axons regenerate in tir-1 mutants compared to wild-type animals.
source: Strikingly, we found that when GABA motor axons of tir-1 loss-of-function and wild-type animals were severed at the midline, significantly more axons regenerated in the absence of tir-1 (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1D showing increased regeneration percentage.

claim: Both tir-1(qd4) and tir-1(tm3036) alleles disrupt the C-terminal TIR domain.
source: We tested two putative null alleles of tir-1; the qd4 allele is a 1078 base pair deletion spanning exons 8–10 and the tm3036 allele is a smaller 269 base pair deletion in exon 8 that results in an early stop codon (Pujol et al., 2008; Shivers et al., 2009). Both the qd4 and tm3036 deletions disrupt the C-terminal toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain, which is essential for TIR-1 function (Chuang and Bargmann, 2005; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by molecular characterization and citations, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The TIR domain is essential for TIR-1 function.
source: Both the qd4 and tm3036 deletions disrupt the C-terminal toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain, which is essential for TIR-1 function (Chuang and Bargmann, 2005; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Axon regeneration is not significantly different in tol-1(nr2033) mutants compared to wild-type controls.
source: We found no significant difference between the number of axons that regenerated in tol-1(nr2033) null mutants and wild-type animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: TIR-1 is a TIR-domain-containing protein with a specific role in axon regeneration.
source: Therefore, TIR-1 is a TIR-domain-containing protein with a specific role in axon regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with tol-1 mutants showing no regeneration phenotype.

claim: TIR-1 inhibits the initiation of axon regeneration and the successful extension of regenerating axons to their targets.
source: Together, these results indicate TIR-1 inhibits the initiation of axon regeneration and the successful extension of regenerating axons to their targets.
evidence: Supported by categorical analysis of regeneration stages in Figure 1F.

claim: C. elegans motor axons do not fuse severed proximal and distal axon fragments.
source: Of note, C. elegans are capable of repairing injured mechanosensory axons both by regenerating and fusing severed proximal and distal axon fragments (Ghosh-Roy et al., 2010; Neumann et al., 2011). However, we did not observe fusion of severed motor axon fragments in either wild-type or tir-1 mutant animals.
evidence: Supported by observation in the study and comparison with cited literature on mechanosensory axons.

claim: Endogenous TIR-1 is expressed in the nervous system, particularly in neurons along the dorsal and ventral nerve cords.
source: With this single-copy integration of mCherry, we observed faint TIR-1 expression in the nervous system, particularly in the nerve ring, select cells in the head and tail, and in the dorsal cord and ventral cord, as well as in the intestine (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by imaging of endogenously tagged TIR-1 in Figure 2A.

claim: TIR-1b::mCherry is expressed in the cell bodies and axons of GABA motor neurons.
source: With this strain, we observed a similar pattern of TIR-1 expression in the intestine and nervous system. However, the increased copy number revealed TIR-1b::mCherry expression in the cell bodies and axons of GABA motor neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by imaging in Figure 2B.

claim: GABA-specific expression of tir-1b rescues axon regeneration in tir-1(qd4) animals.
source: Axon regeneration was fully suppressed in animals that expressed tir-1b specifically in their GABA neurons compared to tir-1(qd4) animals (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 2E.

claim: TIR-1 functions cell-intrinsically to inhibit axon regeneration.
source: Therefore, cell-intrinsic tir-1 function inhibits axon regeneration.
evidence: Supported by GABA-specific rescue experiments.

claim: TIR-1 and human SARM1 proteins are highly conserved, sharing 60% homology over 85% of the SARM1 sequence.
source: TIR-1 and human SARM1 proteins are highly conserved, sharing 60% homology over 85% of the SARM1 sequence (Altschul et al., 1997; Mink et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to sequence analysis.

claim: GABA-specific expression of human SARM1SAM-TIR rescues axon regeneration in tir-1(qd4) mutants.
source: As we observed with tir-1, expressing an active form of human Sarm1 containing its SAM and TIR domains (hSarm1SAMTIR) in GABA motor neurons was sufficient to rescue the regeneration phenotype of tir-1(qd4) mutants (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 2F.

claim: The ability to inhibit axon regeneration cell-autonomously is conserved in the human SARM1SAMTIR protein.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the ability to inhibit axon regeneration cell-autonomously is conserved in the human SARM1SAMTIR protein.
evidence: Supported by human SARM1 rescue experiments.

claim: 90.2% of middle fragments degenerate 24 hr after double axotomy in wild-type axons.
source: In wild-type axons, 90.2% of middle fragments degenerated 24 hr after double axotomy (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 3C.

claim: The observed degeneration is not caused by a release of cytosolic GFP from the severed fragments.
source: We did not observe a significant difference in the number of middle fragments when visualized with either cytosolic or myristoylated and membrane-bound GFP 1.5 hr and 24 hr after injury (Figure 3D), indicating that the observed degeneration is not caused by a release of cytosolic GFP from the severed fragments.
evidence: Supported by comparison of cytosolic and membrane-bound GFP in Figure 3D.

claim: Injured motor axons are less likely to degenerate in aged animals.
source: Finally, we found that injured motor axons are less likely to degenerate in aged animals, indicating an active destruction process is either lost or suppressed with increased age (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by age comparison data in Figure 3F.

claim: The double cut assay reliably induces axon degeneration that can be investigated in vivo and with single-neuron precision.
source: Together, these data indicate that the observed degeneration is an active process, not caused by a leaky cytosolic reporter and that the double cut assay reliably induces axon degeneration that can be investigated in vivo and with single-neuron precision.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental validation.

claim: tir-1 promotes middle fragment degeneration after double injury.
source: We found that in tir-1 mutant animals, only 68% of middle fragments degenerated compared to 86% of middle fragments in wild-type animals (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 3G.

claim: Like Sarm1/dSarm, tir-1 positively regulates injury-induced axon degeneration.
source: Therefore, like Sarm1/dSarm, tir-1 positively regulates injury-induced axon degeneration.
evidence: Supported by degeneration data and comparison with mammalian and fly homologs.

claim: tir-1 functions cell-autonomously to regulate injury-induced axon degeneration.
source: Expression of tir-1b specifically in GABA motor neurons restored middle fragment degeneration in tir-1(qd4) animals, indicating tir-1 functions cell-autonomously to regulate injury-induced axon degeneration (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by GABA-specific rescue of degeneration in Figure 3H.

claim: Middle fragment degeneration after double injury does not depend on ced-1.
source: We found that injured motor axons in ced-1 loss-of-function animals degenerated as frequently as wild-type axons after double axotomy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ced-1 mutant analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: tir-1 functions independently from ced-1 to regulate injury-induced degeneration.
source: Moreover, animals with loss-of-function mutations in both ced-1 and tir-1 phenocopied the amount of degeneration observed in tir-1 animals. These results demonstrate that middle fragment degeneration after double injury does not depend on ced-1 and that tir-1 functions independently from ced-1 to regulate injury-induced degeneration.
evidence: Supported by double mutant analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: C. elegans motor axons have evolved additional as yet unidentified regulators of injury-induced motor axon degeneration.
source: Together with our finding that injury-induced degeneration is not completely dependent on tir-1 (Figure 3F), these data indicate C. elegans motor axons have evolved additional as yet unidentified regulators of injury-induced motor axon degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from incomplete suppression of degeneration in tir-1 mutants.

claim: Low-level expression of GABA-specific TIR-1b causes the majority of distal stumps to degenerate after a single axotomy.
source: Strikingly, we found that low levels of GABA-specific TIR-1b expression caused the majority of distal stumps to degenerate after a single axotomy (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification in Figure 4A-E.

claim: Degeneration was not observed in the proximal stumps after single axotomy in TIR-1b expressing animals.
source: Notably, degeneration was not observed in the proximal stumps, indicating that despite the lack of its autoinhibitory domain, TIR-1 specifically regulates degeneration distal to the site of injury.
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 4A-E.

claim: Overexpressing TIR-1 is sufficient to induce motor axon degeneration in the absence of injury.
source: To further investigate the extent to which TIR-1 is able to promote axon degeneration, we asked whether overexpressing TIR-1 is sufficient to induce motor axon degeneration in the absence of injury. When we expressed tir-1b at high concentrations, we found that GFP-labeled motor axons were beaded, severely fragmented, and degenerated even in the absence of injury (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification in Figure 4F-K.

claim: tir-1 overexpression selectively induces axon degeneration and not cell death.
source: Despite the absence of axons, the number of GABA neuron cell bodies was consistent between transgenic and non-transgenic animals, indicating tir-1 overexpression selectively induces axon degeneration and not cell death (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by cell body counts in Figure 4G.

claim: Elevated tir-1b expression within GABA neurons is sufficient to induce severe and chronic axon degeneration, even in the absence of injury.
source: Therefore, elevated tir-1b expression within GABA neurons is sufficient to induce severe and chronic axon degeneration, even in the absence of injury.
evidence: Supported by overexpression experiments.

claim: tir-1 positively regulates axon degeneration when it is constitutively activated or sufficiently activated by injury.
source: Together with the finding that loss of tir-1 function suppresses injury-induced axon degeneration, these data demonstrate that tir-1 positively regulates axon degeneration when it is constitutively activated or sufficiently activated by injury.
evidence: Supported by loss-of-function and overexpression data.

claim: Axons regenerate significantly less frequently after a double injury compared to a single injury.
source: Indeed, the importance of comparing aspects of the injury response within the same injury model is manifest in the finding that axons regenerate significantly less frequently after a double injury compared to a single injury (60.53% of axons regenerate in the 24 hr following a single injury, and 37.38% of axons regenerate in the 24 hr following a double injury).
evidence: Supported by comparison of regeneration frequencies between single and double injury models.

claim: The NAD+ hydrolase activity of SARM1 is conserved in the C. elegans TIR domain.
source: The NAD+ hydrolase activity of SARM1 is conserved in the C. elegans TIR domain, in a TIR-1 isoform lacking the N-terminal inhibitory domain, and in the full-length TIR-1 protein (Gerdts et al., 2016; Horsefield et al., 2019; Loring et al., 2021; Loring et al., 2020; Peterson et al., 2022; Summers et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The conserved E788/E642 catalytic residue is required for the NADase activity of the TIR-1, SARM1, and dSarm TIR domains.
source: The conserved E788/E642/E1170 catalytic residue is required for the NADase activity of the TIR-1, SARM1, and dSarm TIR domains (Brace et al., 2022; Essuman et al., 2017; Herrmann et al., 2022; Horsefield et al., 2019; Hsu et al., 2021; Loring et al., 2021; Peterson et al., 2022; Summers et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: tir-1(E788A) and tir-1(D773A) mutant animals displayed wild-type levels of axon regeneration.
source: We found that both tir-1(E788A) and tir-1(D773A) mutant animals displayed wild-type levels of axon regeneration, indicating that TIR-1E788A and TIR-1D773A are functionally expressed and that neither residue are required for TIR-1 to inhibit axon regeneration (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by regeneration data in Figure 5A.

claim: TIR-1 regulates regeneration independently of its NADase activity.
source: Therefore, TIR-1 regulates regeneration independently of its NADase activity.
evidence: Supported by E788A mutation not affecting regeneration.

claim: DLK-1 function is absolutely required for the regeneration of otherwise wild-type GABA motor axons.
source: Perhaps the most deterministic regulator of axon regeneration in C. elegans motor neurons is the mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase DLK-1 (Dual leucine zipper kinase-1). DLK-1 function is absolutely required for the regeneration of otherwise wild-type GABA motor axons (Hammarlund et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of tir-1 function did not suppress the complete absence of regeneration in dlk-1 or pmk-3 loss-of-function mutants.
source: We found that loss of tir-1 function did not suppress the complete absence of regeneration in either the dlk-1 loss-of-function mutant or the downstream pmk-3/p38 MAPK loss-of-function mutant, indicating tir-1 either functions upstream of dlk-1 signaling or in a separate signaling pathway (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 5B.

claim: TIR-1 does not function downstream of, or redundantly with, DLK-1 to regulate axon regeneration.
source: However, the genetic interactions do indicate that TIR-1 does not function downstream of, or redundantly with, DLK-1 to regulate axon regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis analysis.

claim: Loss of nsy-1 or pmk-1 enhanced axon regeneration after double injury.
source: We first asked whether TIR-1 regulates axon regeneration by interacting with the NSY-1 signal transduction pathway and found that loss of nsy-1 or its downstream MAP kinase pmk-1/p38 enhanced axon regeneration after double injury (Figure 5C and F).
evidence: Supported by regeneration data in Figure 5C.

claim: tir-1, nsy-1, and pmk-1 function in the same pathway to regulate axon regeneration after double injury.
source: Because tir-1, nsy-1, and pmk-1 null mutants all inhibit axon regeneration to the same extent, and because the amount of regeneration in any pairwise combination of mutants is not additive or multiplicative compared to the single mutants, our data indicate that the three genes function in the same pathway to regulate axon regeneration after double injury (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by genetic epistasis analysis in Figure 5C and F.

claim: unc-43(e408) phenocopied the increased axon regeneration of tir-1(qd4) mutants.
source: We found that unc-43(e408) phenocopied the increased axon regeneration of tir-1(qd4) mutants and addition of the unc-43(e408) mutation to tir-1(qd4) mutants did not further enhance regeneration (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 5D.

claim: tir-1 and unc-43 function together in a shared genetic pathway to inhibit axon regeneration after double injury.
source: Therefore, tir-1 and unc-43 function together in a shared genetic pathway to inhibit axon regeneration after double injury.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis analysis.

claim: Loss of daf-19 function increased regeneration to the same extent as loss of tir-1.
source: However, loss of daf-19 function increased regeneration to the same extent as loss of tir-1 and did not enhance the regeneration phenotype of the tir-1 null mutants (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 5E.

claim: An unc-43/tir-1/nsy-1/pmk-1/daf-19 signaling cascade inhibits axon regeneration by altering transcription of downstream regeneration-associated genes.
source: Together, these data are consistent with a model in which an unc-43/tir-1/nsy-1/pmk-1/daf-19 signaling cascade (Figure 5E) inhibits axon regeneration by altering transcription of downstream regeneration-associated genes.
evidence: Inferred from genetic pathway analysis and involvement of transcription factor DAF-19.

claim: The E788A/E642A mutation did not suppress injury-induced axon degeneration.
source: Interestingly, the E788A/E642A mutation did not suppress injury-induced axon degeneration (Figure 6A), indicating TIR-1 can regulate axon degeneration independently of its NAD+ hydrolase activity.
evidence: Supported by degeneration data in Figure 6A.

claim: TIR-1 regulates a previously unexplored mechanism of axon degeneration.
source: This ability contrasts sharply with the requirement for NAD+ hydrolysis in dSarm and SARM1-mediated degeneration (Brace et al., 2022; Essuman et al., 2017; Gerdts et al., 2015; Herrmann et al., 2022; Hsu et al., 2021), indicating TIR-1 regulates a previously unexplored mechanism of axon degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with mammalian and fly SARM proteins.

claim: Axon degeneration in tir-1(D773A) mutants was slightly but significantly disrupted compared to wild-type animals.
source: We found that axon degeneration in tir-1(D773A) mutants was slightly but significantly disrupted compared to wild-type animals and was similar to that seen in tir-1(qd4) animals (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by degeneration data in Figure 6A.

claim: The SS loop is important for TIR-1's ability to promote degeneration of injured axons.
source: These data indicate the SS loop is important for TIR-1's ability to promote degeneration of injured axons.
evidence: Inferred from D773A mutation affecting degeneration.

claim: TIR-1 regulates axon regeneration and degeneration by different mechanisms.
source: Notably, D773A/D627A is not a null mutation since it did not disrupt the ability of TIR-1 to inhibit regeneration (Figure 5A). It follows that TIR-1 regulates axon regeneration and degeneration by different mechanisms, potentially by directly interacting with components of the UNC-43-NSY-1-PMK-1 pathway on the proximal side of the injury and another signal transduction pathway on the distal side of the injury.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of D773A mutation on regeneration vs degeneration.

claim: Expressing large amounts of wild-type tir-1b induced significant axon degeneration even in the absence of injury, but expressing tir-1b(E788A) or tir-1b(D773A) did not.
source: We found that while expressing large amounts of wild-type tir-1b induced significant axon degeneration even in the absence of injury, expressing either tir-1b(E788A/E642A) or tir-1b(D773A/D627A) did not (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by chronic degeneration data in Figure 6B.

claim: D773 is required for both injury-induced and spontaneous degeneration.
source: Together with our previous results, we find that D773 is required for both injury-induced and spontaneous degeneration, while E788 is only required for spontaneous degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of mutations in different degeneration contexts.

claim: The NADase activity of TIR-1 is required to induce spontaneous degeneration when overexpressed in uninjured axons but is not required for degeneration of injured axon fragments.
source: These data indicate D773A disrupts multiple facets of TIR-1 function, and the NADase activity of TIR-1 is required to induce spontaneous degeneration when overexpressed in uninjured axons but is not required for degeneration of injured axon fragments.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of injury-induced and spontaneous degeneration requirements.

claim: Loss of pmk-1 did not have a degeneration phenotype on its own.
source: Loss of pmk-1 did not have a degeneration phenotype on its own and double tir-1; pmk-1 mutant animals phenocopied the degeneration observed in tir-1 mutant animals (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 7A.

claim: tir-1 functions independently from pmk-1 to promote axon degeneration after injury.
source: This lack of genetic interaction indicates that tir-1 functions independently from pmk-1 to promote axon degeneration after injury.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis analysis.

claim: Loss of dlk-1 or pmk-3 function did not affect axon degeneration on their own.
source: In our assay, loss of either dlk-1 or its downstream p38 MAP kinase pmk-3 did not affect axon degeneration on their own; however, they did rescue axon degeneration in tir-1 mutants (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 7B.

claim: The decreased axon degeneration phenotype of tir-1 mutants depends on dlk-1 pathway activity.
source: This result suggests the decreased axon degeneration phenotype of tir-1 mutants depends on dlk-1 pathway activity.
evidence: Inferred from genetic suppression analysis.

claim: Significantly less severed axon fragments degenerated in dlk-1(oe) animals relative to wild-type animals.
source: We found that, indeed, significantly less severed axon fragments degenerated in dlk-1(oe) animals relative to wild-type animals (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by overexpression data in Figure 7B and C.

claim: DLK-1's ability to inhibit degeneration is context specific.
source: Of note, DLK-1 function is not responsible for inhibiting degeneration after a single injury as neither loss or gain of dlk-1 function induced degeneration of singly injured distal axon fragments (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). Therefore, DLK-1's ability to inhibit degeneration is context specific.
evidence: Supported by comparison of single and double injury in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of pmk-3/p38 MAPK function rescued degeneration in both dlk-1(oe) and tir-1(-) animals, as well as in double dlk-1(oe); tir-1(-) mutants.
source: However, loss of pmk-3/p38 MAPK function rescued degeneration in both dlk-1(oe) and tir-1(-) animals, as well as in double dlk-1(oe); tir-1(-) mutants (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by genetic epistasis data in Figure 7B.

claim: PMK-3 inhibits degeneration downstream of its canonical MAPKKK DLK-1, and also functions downstream of TIR-1.
source: The simplest interpretation of these genetic epistasis analyses is that PMK-3 inhibits degeneration downstream of its canonical MAPKKK DLK-1, and also functions downstream of TIR-1.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis analysis.

claim: TIR-1 promotes degeneration by antagonizing or opposing the inhibitory role of DLK-1-PMK-3 signaling.
source: These findings support a model in which TIR-1 promotes degeneration by antagonizing or opposing the inhibitory role of DLK-1-PMK-3 signaling.
evidence: Inferred from genetic interaction patterns.

claim: TIR-1 promotes axon degeneration by directly or indirectly antagonizing DLK-1-PMK-3 function on the distal side of the injury and inhibits regeneration with UNC-43–NSY-1–PMK-1–DAF-19 signaling on the proximal side of the injury.
source: Together, our data indicate that TIR-1 promotes axon degeneration by directly or indirectly antagonizing DLK-1-PMK-3 function on the distal side of the injury and inhibits regeneration with UNC-43–NSY-1–PMK-1–DAF-19 signaling on the proximal side of the injury (Figure 7D).
evidence: Summary of genetic pathway analysis, illustrated in Figure 7D.

claim: TIR-1/SARM1/dSarm is a central regulator of axon degeneration and a previously uncharacterized intrinsic inhibitor of axon regeneration.
source: Here, we identify TIR-1/SARM1/dSarm, a central regulator of axon degeneration, as a previously uncharacterized intrinsic inhibitor of axon regeneration that can be targeted to increase repair of injured motor axons.
evidence: Summary statement supported by all experimental findings.

claim: tir-1 inhibits axon regeneration with the NSY-1–PMK-1 MAPK pathway on the proximal side of the injury while it promotes degeneration by antagonizing the DLK-1–PMK-3 MAPK pathway on the distal side of the injury.
source: Our data indicate that to achieve this specificity of function, tir-1 inhibits axon regeneration with the NSY-1–PMK-1 MAPK pathway on the proximal side of the injury while it promotes degeneration by antagonizing the DLK-1–PMK-3 MAPK pathway on the distal side of the injury.
evidence: Summary of genetic pathway analysis.

claim: Both tir-1 and human Sarm1 can function cell-autonomously to inhibit axon regeneration.
source: The finding that both tir-1 and human Sarm1 can function cell-autonomously to inhibit axon regeneration indicates intrinsic regulation of axon regeneration may be a conserved function of SARM proteins.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with both TIR-1 and human SARM1.

claim: The increased regeneration of tir-1 mutants is not a secondary consequence of a decrease in degeneration.
source: Here, we found that axons lacking tir-1 regenerate more often than wild-type axons after a single injury even though a single injury does not cause degeneration in either wild-type or tir-1 mutants. Thus, the increased regeneration of tir-1 mutants is not a secondary consequence of a decrease in degeneration.
evidence: Supported by comparison of regeneration after single injury where degeneration does not occur.

claim: tir-1 functions within the proximal fragments of injured axons to inhibit axon regeneration independently from its role in degeneration.
source: Combined with our finding that tir-1 functions within GABA axons to regulate axon regeneration, our data suggest that tir-1 functions within the proximal fragments of injured axons to inhibit axon regeneration independently from its role in degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from cell-autonomous function and independence from degeneration.

claim: TIR-1/SARM1 functions with UNC-43/CAMKII, the NSY-1/ASK1–PMK-1/p38 MAPK signaling cascade, and the transcription factor DAF-19/RFX to inhibit axon regeneration.
source: On the proximal side, TIR-1/SARM1 functions with UNC-43/CAMKII, the NSY-1/ASK1–PMK-1/p38 MAPK signaling cascade, and the transcription factor DAF-19/RFX to inhibit axon regeneration.
evidence: Supported by genetic epistasis analysis.

claim: The involvement of DAF-19 suggests that TIR-1 activation may change the transcriptional profile of the proximal fragment into one that does not support repair.
source: The involvement of DAF-19 suggests that TIR-1 activation may change the transcriptional profile of the proximal fragment into one that does not support repair.
evidence: Inferred from DAF-19 being a transcription factor in the pathway.

claim: DAF-19 does not require the co-transcription factor ATF-7 to regulate axon regeneration.
source: Unlike the TIR-1–NSY-1–PMK-1 pathway that regulates the innate immune response and serotonin biosynthesis, DAF-19 does not require the co-transcription factor ATF-7 to regulate axon regeneration (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by lack of atf-7 phenotype in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and citation.

claim: SARM1 has been found to regulate a c-Jun-mediated transcriptional program and an immune response in injured mammalian axons.
source: SARM1 has been found to regulate a c-Jun-mediated transcriptional program and an immune response in injured mammalian axons (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The role of tir-1 in axon regeneration does not depend on its ability hydrolyze NAD+.
source: The additional finding that axon regeneration is not affected by mutation in the predicted NADase residue E788A/E642A suggests that the role of tir-1 in axon regeneration does not depend on its ability hydrolyze NAD+.
evidence: Supported by E788A mutation data.

claim: dSarm regulates neuromuscular junction formation and glial phagocytosis using both its NADase activity and interaction with Ask1 signaling.
source: TIR-1's ability to regulate regeneration in coordination with NSY-1 signaling and independently of its NADase activity contrasts with recent findings that dSarm regulates neuromuscular junction formation and glial phagocytosis using both its NADase activity and interaction with Ask1 signaling (Brace et al., 2022; Herrmann et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: dSarm, mSarm, and hSARM1 rely on their ability to hydrolyze NAD+ to regulate axon degeneration.
source: The NADase-independent function of TIR-1 also contrasts with the findings that dSarm, mSarm, and hSARM1 rely on their ability to hydrolyze NAD+ to regulate axon degeneration (Brace et al., 2022; Herrmann et al., 2022; Hsu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: dSarm regulates axon transport within uninjured bystander neurons independently of its NADase activity and by interacting with the voltage-gated calcium channel Cacophony (Cac) and Ask1/NSY-1 MAPK signaling.
source: However, the TIR-1 mechanism parallels the mechanism by which dSarm regulates axon transport within uninjured bystander neurons, which occurs independently of its NADase activity and by interacting with the voltage-gated calcium channel Cacophony (Cac) and Ask1/NSY-1 MAPK signaling (Hsu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: dSarm and tir-1 can regulate multiple components of the injury response independently of NAD+ hydrolysis.
source: These data indicate that dSarm and tir-1 can regulate multiple components of the injury response independently of NAD+ hydrolysis.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of NADase-independent functions.

claim: NMNAT antagonizes SARM1 by maintaining NAD+ in the allosteric pocket of SARM1, which inhibits its NAD+ hydrolase activity.
source: NMNAT antagonizes SARM1 by maintaining NAD+ in the allosteric pocket of SARM1, which inhibits its NAD+ hydrolase activity (Bratkowski et al., 2020; Figley et al., 2021; Horsefield et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2020; Sasaki et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2022; Sporny et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMNAT2 inhibits axon regeneration in C. elegans mechanosensory axons.
source: Previous work demonstrates that NMNAT2 inhibits axon regeneration in C. elegans mechanosensory axons (Kim et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: TIR-1 inhibits regeneration of motor axons independently of its function as an NAD+ hydrolase.
source: However, here we find that TIR-1 inhibits regeneration of motor axons independently of its function as an NAD+ hydrolase, indicating that NMNAT-2 must not inhibit regeneration by suppressing the NADase activity of TIR-1.
evidence: Inferred from E788A mutation not affecting regeneration.

claim: Loss of pmk-1 function has no effect on axon degeneration.
source: Loss of pmk-1 function has no effect on axon degeneration, nor does it affect the degeneration phenotype of tir-1 loss-of-function mutants, indicating that TIR-1 regulates axon degeneration independently from the NSY-1–PMK-1 MAPK pathway.
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 7A.

claim: TIR-1 regulates axon degeneration independently from the NSY-1–PMK-1 MAPK pathway.
source: Loss of pmk-1 function has no effect on axon degeneration, nor does it affect the degeneration phenotype of tir-1 loss-of-function mutants, indicating that TIR-1 regulates axon degeneration independently from the NSY-1–PMK-1 MAPK pathway.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis analysis.

claim: TIR-1 promotes injury-induced degeneration by inhibiting a protective function of DLK-1 and PMK-3.
source: Specifically, our data suggest that in C. elegans, TIR-1 promotes injury-induced degeneration by inhibiting a protective function of DLK-1 and PMK-3.
evidence: Inferred from genetic interaction patterns.

claim: Wallenda (Wnd), the DLK-1 homolog in Drosophila melanogaster inhibits axon degeneration in motor axons that have undergone a conditioning lesion.
source: The protective function of DLK-1 and PMK-3 in axon degeneration appears to be conserved in specific contexts. For example, Wallenda (Wnd), the DLK-1 homolog in Drosophila melanogaster inhibits axon degeneration in motor axons that have undergone a conditioning lesion (Xiong and Collins, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Wallenda promotes degeneration in singly severed olfactory receptor axons and mammalian DLK promotes degeneration of severed dorsal root ganglion axons.
source: However, Wallenda also promotes degeneration in singly severed olfactory receptor axons and mammalian DLK promotes degeneration of severed dorsal root ganglion axons (Ghosh et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SARM1 and dSarm regulate axon degeneration by interacting with the signaling pathways of DLK-1 homologs Wallenda and DLK.
source: In relation to SARM signaling, SARM1 and dSarm also regulate axon degeneration by interacting with the signaling pathways of DLK-1 homologs Wallenda and DLK (Summers et al., 2020; Walker et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MAPK signaling functions downstream of SARM1 to regulate degeneration of crushed retinal ganglion cells.
source: Separate studies have found that MAPK signaling functions downstream of SARM1 to regulate degeneration of crushed retinal ganglion cells and upstream of SARM1 to regulate degeneration of cultured mammalian dorsal root ganglia neurons and Drosophila motoneurons (Summers et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The highly conserved TIR-1, dSarm, and SARM1 proteins regulate injury-induced degeneration through interactions with shared MAPK signaling components.
source: Together with this multifaceted relationship between SARM1 and MAPK signaling, our data indicate the highly conserved TIR-1, dSarm, and SARM1 proteins regulate injury-induced degeneration through interactions with shared MAPK signaling components.
evidence: Inferred from comparison across species and current findings.

claim: The precise interactions between TIR-1/SARM1/dSarm and DLK-1/MAPK/Wnd signaling are complex and likely depend on cell type, form of injury, and species.
source: However, the precise interactions between TIR-1/SARM1/dSarm and DLK-1/MAPK/Wnd signaling are complex and likely depend on cell type, form of injury, and species.
evidence: Inferred from variability in reported interactions across different studies.

claim: TIR-1 is required for degeneration in a C. elegans model of ALS.
source: In addition to regulating the injury response, TIR-1 is required for degeneration in a C. elegans model of ALS, functions in the epidermis to promote age-dependent degeneration of PVD dendrites, induces spontaneous degeneration when forced to multimerize, and inhibits spontaneous axon degeneration of PVQ interneurons in mutant ric-7(-) animals, which lack mitochondria (Ding et al., 2022; Lezi et al., 2018; Loring et al., 2021; Rawson et al., 2014; Vérièpe et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: pmk-3 inhibits spontaneous degeneration in the absence of mitochondria.
source: Interestingly, pmk-3 was also found to inhibit spontaneous degeneration in the absence of mitochondria, suggesting the difference between promotion and suppression of degeneration may ultimately be attributed to differential regulation of PMK-3 in these two contexts.
evidence: Supported by comparison with prior literature on mitochondrial degeneration.

claim: C. elegans does not have an identifiable Axundead homolog.
source: C. elegans does not have an identifiable Axundead homolog; however, the NADase activity of SARM1 and dSarm is conserved, albeit perhaps to a weaker extent, in the C. elegans TIR domain (Horsefield et al., 2019; Loring et al., 2020; Neukomm et al., 2017; Peterson et al., 2022; Summers et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: E788A renders the C. elegans TIR domain catalytically dead and is required for TIR-1-mediated pathogen avoidance.
source: Our finding that TIR-1 can promote injury-induced degeneration despite having a E788A/E642A mutation in its key catalytic residue, along with a recent finding that E788A renders the C. elegans TIR domain catalytically dead and is required for TIR-1-mediated pathogen avoidance, indicates that although TIR-1 does function as an NADase, it regulates injury-induced axon degeneration independently of its NADase activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: TIR-1 does function as an NADase.
source: Our finding that TIR-1 can promote injury-induced degeneration despite having a E788A/E642A mutation in its key catalytic residue, along with a recent finding that E788A renders the C. elegans TIR domain catalytically dead and is required for TIR-1-mediated pathogen avoidance, indicates that although TIR-1 does function as an NADase, it regulates injury-induced axon degeneration independently of its NADase activity.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature showing NADase activity.

claim: TIR-1 regulates injury induced degeneration independently of its NADase activity.
source: Our finding that TIR-1 can promote injury-induced degeneration despite having a E788A/E642A mutation in its key catalytic residue, along with a recent finding that E788A renders the C. elegans TIR domain catalytically dead and is required for TIR-1-mediated pathogen avoidance, indicates that although TIR-1 does function as an NADase, it regulates injury-induced axon degeneration independently of its NADase activity.
evidence: Supported by E788A mutation not affecting injury-induced degeneration.

claim: While TIR-1 can promote NADase-independent degeneration, dSarm and SARM1 depend on NAD+ hydrolysis to regulate injury-induced degeneration.
source: While TIR-1 can promote NADase-independent degeneration, dSarm and SARM1 depend on NAD+ hydrolysis to regulate injury-induced degeneration (Brace et al., 2022; Herrmann et al., 2022; Hsu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: While TIR-1 does not require its NADase activity to promote injury-induced degeneration, it can use its enzymatic activity to induce spontaneous axon degeneration.
source: Interestingly, while overexpressing wild-type tir-1b in motor neurons induced spontaneous degeneration, expressing the same amount of mutant tir-1b, containing the D773A or E788A mutation, did not induce significant degeneration. Therefore, while TIR-1 does not require its NADase activity to promote injury-induced degeneration, it can use its enzymatic activity to induce spontaneous axon degeneration.
evidence: Supported by differential effects of mutations in injury-induced vs spontaneous degeneration.

claim: TIR-1 has evolved dual mechanisms to regulate degeneration in response to different insults that it encounters in the wild.
source: These data suggest that TIR-1 has evolved dual mechanisms to regulate degeneration in response to different insults that it encounters in the wild.
evidence: Inferred from NADase-dependent and independent mechanisms.

claim: Systemic inhibition of tir-1/Sarm1 increases axon regeneration after injury in zebrafish.
source: Recent studies support the idea that SARM orthologs might function intrinsically to directly regulate axon regeneration. Systemic inhibition of tir-1/Sarm1 increases axon regeneration after injury in zebrafish.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Functional recovery and axon regeneration after injury is improved in the absence of SARM1 function in neurons and in astrocytes, in part due to reduced inflammation and increased protection of injured axons.
source: In addition, a mammalian study suggests functional recovery and axon regeneration after injury is improved in the absence of SARM1 function in neurons and in astrocytes, in part due to reduced inflammation and increased protection of injured axons (Asgharsharghi et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SARM1 function within injured axons regulates an immune response that triggers inflammation.
source: This data is supported by a preceding finding that SARM1 function within injured axons regulates an immune response that triggers inflammation (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SARM1 knockout mice have more collateral axon branching and increased cytoskeletal dynamics in postnatal sensory neurons.
source: Another recent study demonstrated that SARM1 knockout mice have more collateral axon branching and increased cytoskeletal dynamics in postnatal sensory neurons, indicating that SARM1 inhibits axon growth even in the absence of injury (Ketschek et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SARM1 inhibits axon growth even in the absence of injury.
source: Another recent study demonstrated that SARM1 knockout mice have more collateral axon branching and increased cytoskeletal dynamics in postnatal sensory neurons, indicating that SARM1 inhibits axon growth even in the absence of injury (Ketschek et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.
